articles.body: CHANDIGARH: A Chandigarh Police head constable was found dead with a gunshot injury to his head at his government accommodation in Sector 22 on Friday morning, with police investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident. Deceased son Arman is the main suspect behind the murder. Police rounded up Arman and interrogating him.The deceased was identified as Nitin, who was posted in the Accounts Branch at the Chandigarh police headquarters in Sector 9. His wife is also posted as an ASI with Chandigarh police.According to preliminary information, Nitin, his wife and their son were present at the house when the incident took place. Around 7 am, the head constable’s wife reportedly went to the terrace and raised an alarm, following which neighbours gathered at the spot.When people entered the house, Nitin was found lying on a bed in a pool of blood. He had sustained a serious gunshot injury to his head. Police said the circumstances leading to the firing were yet to be established.A country-made pistol was recovered from the spot. Police teams are examining CCTV footage from the surrounding area and questioning family members, including the couple’s son, as part of the investigation.On receiving information, Chandigarh Police SSP Kanwardeep Kaur, SP Crime Anurag Daru and station house officers of police stations under the Central Division reached the spot. The officers inspected the government accommodation and the scene of the incident.Police are investigating whether the firing was accidental, self-inflicted or involved any other circumstances. articles.title: About 51,000 battery packs used inside reclining chairs are being recalled after reports of overheating, smoking and igniting; the packs were sold on Amazon for about $105 for more than three years
articles.summary: The U.S.
articles.body: The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) has recalled approximately 51,000 lithium-ion battery packs used in reclining chairs after reports of the batteries overheating and catching fire. The recalled product is Blue Cactus Company's 2,500 mAh battery pack (model RWX-RBP02), which was sold on Amazon from May 2023 through July 2026.The agency said it received four reports of the batteries overheating, smoking or igniting. Though there are only a small number of reported cases, lithium-ion batteries still carry dangers when they fail. They can ignite suddenly and are difficult to extinguish once they start burning. The recall announcement was made on Thursday (September 24).How to identify the recalled batteryThe recalled products are black battery packs with ‘The Blue Cactus Company’ branding and logo printed on the front. The recalled product bears the model number RWX-RBP02 on the rear. These batteries were designed to power various reclining chair brands, meaning they may have been sold alongside different manufacturers' furniture or as replacement parts.If you purchased a reclining chair battery pack from Amazon between May 2023 and July 2026 for around $105, it is important that you check the battery against the model number. The product is fairly distinctive: it comes with a black casing, and the branding is unmistakable. Look for the model number to know whether your battery falls under this recall.What should you do?If your recliner has the recalled battery, it is important that you stop using it right away and contact The Blue Cactus Company for a replacement. The company said it is offering free replacements for the recalled product. You may need to reference your purchase receipt or product information when reaching out.In the meantime, remove the battery pack from your reclining chair and store it away from living areas, ideally in a cool, dry place away from other flammable materials.“Do not throw this recalled lithium-ion battery or device in the trash, the general recycling stream (e.g., street-level or kerbside recycling bins), or in used battery recycling boxes found at various retail and home improvement stores,” the CPSC said.The agency urged that the recalled lithium-ion batteries must be disposed of differently from other batteries, as they present a greater risk of fire. “Your municipal household hazardous waste (HHW) collection centre may accept this recalled lithium-ion battery or device for disposal. Before taking your battery or device to a HHW collection centre, contact it ahead of time and ask whether it accepts recalled lithium-ion batteries. If it does not, contact your municipality for further guidance,” the agency added.The recalled battery packs were imported by Go North Rocket 28 AB, a company based in Sweden. They were sold exclusively through Amazon during the three-year window. You can contact the manufacturer directly or work through Amazon customer service if you still have your order history.If you have the recalled batteries, the safest approach is to treat them as a potential hazard until you have obtained a replacement. Check your Amazon order history if you cannot recall whether you own one of these packs. The model number RWX-RBP02 is the specific identifier to verify. If you find one in your home, do not use it, and begin the process of getting it replaced and properly disposed of.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Staying home can’t be our safety policy', women take to the streets in Delhi
articles.summary: Reached?
articles.body: Reached? – The question women’s safety begins and ends withAnusha Garg, a third-year journalism student and President of the LSR Students’ Union, expresses what every woman occupying public spaces in Delhi feels:This week, after a minor was reportedly gang- raped in a South Delhi, my first instinct was: safety had to come first. But I kept returning to the one contradiction – the danger was outside, yet we were the ones being asked to retreat.Women’s safety is not something we discuss only after a disturbing headline. It is built into our everyday plans. Among friends, “reached?” is almost a form of punctuation. If a college event ends late, the conversation changes quickly, “Metro or cab? Is that road crowded? Should we leave together? Share your location. Call when you reach”. These calculations become so routine that we barely register them. But there is a thin line between protection and restriction. “Come home early” can become the answer to a problem women did not create.National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data show that 13,396 crimes against women were registered in Delhi in 2024. Registered crime is not the same as the full prevalence of violence, but the figure makes it impossible to dismiss the anxiety women carry through the city. And that anxiety has a cost.A spontaneous evening out for a male friend comes with logistical queries for us: route, transport, company, phone battery, one last message home. “Stay home” cannot be our final safety policy. If women withdraw whenever public spaces feel unsafe, those spaces do not become safer; they simply become devoid of women. I will still share my location. I will still text “reached”. Precautions matter. But a safe city cannot be one where women become experts at disappearing. It has to be one where our presence requires no explanation.- As told to Sara SiddiquiYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Oregon feared a famous 92-foot waterfall on private land could be sold to a new owner; the state has now approved a $2 million purchase that will permanently protect Abiqua Falls and open public access
articles.summary: Oregon has approved a $2 million purchase of Abiqua Falls, ending concerns that the famous 92-foot waterfall could remain in private hands after its owner
articles.body: Oregon has approved a $2 million purchase of Abiqua Falls, ending concerns that the famous 92-foot waterfall could remain in private hands after its owner put the property up for sale earlier this year. The deal includes the waterfall and 160 acres of land in Marion County, with the state planning to protect the site and provide public access.The Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission approved the sale from the Abbey Foundation of Oregon on Wednesday, KGW8 reported. The foundation had owned the property for more than 100 years and put it up for sale in February, raising concerns among members of the public and lawmakers about what could happen to the popular natural landmark if it went to another private owner.Abiqua Falls is located near Scotts Mills, east of Salem. The waterfall drops 92 feet into a pool surrounded by ferns, moss-covered rocks and a basalt cliff. People have visited the site for decades even though the land itself was privately owned.The agreement now moves the property towards public ownership. The purchase is expected to close around the end of 2026, according to Oregon State Parks and Recreation Department (OPRD). The agency is also working on options for how the property will be managed and developed.The sale of Abiqua Falls The Abbey Foundation of Oregon, the fundraising organisation connected to Mount Angel Abbey and Seminary, had owned Abiqua Falls for more than a century. When the property was listed for sale in February, Oregon lawmakers moved to find a way to keep the waterfall in public hands.An earlier proposal reported by Oregon Public Broadcasting included $2.1 million for the acquisition. That proposal covered $600,000 for the Abiqua Falls property and $1.4 million for another 160 acres of nearby rapids and forestland owned by timber company Weyerhaeuser.The latest agreement approved by the Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission is for $2 million and includes the 92-foot waterfall and 160 acres of unmaintained trails.The Abbey Foundation said it was handing over responsibility for the site with the hope that it would remain accessible for future generations."It is with deep gratitude and hope for the future that the Abbey Foundation of Oregon entrusts the stewardship and legacy of Abiqua Falls to the state of Oregon,” said Dr Amanda Staggenborg, director of communications for Mount Angel Abbey. "The beauty of Abiqua Falls will be enjoyed by generations of Oregonians and all those who love Oregon’s natural wonders," she added.Lawmakers backed public ownershipThe effort to acquire the waterfall received support from lawmakers from both political parties. They pursued the purchase through a general obligation bond to bring the property into public ownership.House Majority Leader Ben Bowman said the purchase would allow future generations to visit the waterfall themselves. "Today, we are making sure that our children and grandchildren inherit not just stories about Abiqua Falls, but the ability to stand there themselves," Bowman said. "This place should belong to all of us. Oregon owes a debt of gratitude to the Abbey Foundation for their century of stewardship, and their partnership in ensuring public access forever," he added.The move followed months of discussion about the future of the waterfall after its sale was proposed. Earlier in March, lawmakers had said several details still needed to be settled, including which state agency would manage the property and how public access would work.State has to prepare the siteBuying the waterfall is only the beginning of bringing the property under state management. The land currently includes unmaintained trails, meaning the state will have to determine how the site can be managed and brought up to the standards expected of a public park.OPRD director Lisa Sumption said owning a natural site also means taking on the work needed to maintain it. "Abiqua Falls is a great example that parks are not just nature. It takes continuous staff, time and money for us to bring a property like this up to state park standards and keep it there," Sumption said.The agency has not yet announced a final management plan for the property. articles.title: Derry-Dublin flight route: Operator yet to be appointed
articles.summary: It is unclear when the new service between the two cities will begin, with doubts raised about the planned October start date.
articles.body:
No operator has yet been appointed for the new Londonderry-Dublin flight service, raising doubts over a proposed October start date.

In May, the Irish Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien told the Dáil (the lower house of the Irish parliament) that the service was expected to begin in October.

The actual start date is now unclear, with a spokesperson for City of Derry Airport (CODA) saying it is continuing to work closely with the Republic of Ireland's Department of Transport to progress the service.

It will be funded under a public service obligation (PSO) scheme, where governments support flights that would not otherwise be commercially viable.

A daily service between City of Derry Airport and Dublin, funded by the Irish government, was withdrawn in 2011 and attempts to revive the service faltered in 2016.

Last year, the Irish government said it hoped to reinstate the route by the end of 2026 after announcing in November that it was investing €2m (£1.76m) to get flights from Dublin to Londonderry up and running next year.

It announced more than €50m (£44m) worth of funding for projects as part of the Shared Island initiative.

Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Friday, Sinn Féin Donegal TD Pádraig Mac Lochlainn said it was "frustrating that the target date of October has been delayed".

"I received another parliamentary response yesterday [Thursday], and what the minister is saying is that because City of Derry operates outside of the European Union, the public service obligation air service has to operate outside of European Union regulations.

"So he is taking advice from the chief state solicitor's office and the office of the attorney general, and they are saying they are very close to issuing a request for tenders.

"Hopefully this happens very, very soon and I have been in contact with the team at City of Derry Airport and they are still very hopeful that this can happen before the end of the year."

Mac Lochlainn said the process had clearly been "complicated" by Brexit.

"That being said, I do think this should have been resolved by now," he said.

In a statement, the Republic of Ireland's Department of Transport said it anticipates "being in a position to publish a request for tenders (RfT) document very shortly".

The tender process will allow airlines to compete for the contract to operate the route.

The department said it hopes to award the contract this year, saying they hope services can begin "as soon as operationally feasible" once an operator has been appointed.

articles.title: The Trump-Xi meeting was heavy on pomp, light on substance. China is just fine with that
articles.summary: Four months after their last meeting, President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping traded niceties during the Chinese leader’s first visit to the US capital in over a decade.
articles.body: Four months after their last meeting, President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping traded niceties during the Chinese leader’s first visit to the US capital in over a decade. The two leaders extended a trade truce, exchanged gifts and compliments, and acknowledged the possibility of working together to contain the dangers of AI development. For a historic summit meant to address rising tensions between the world’s largest economic and geopolitical powers, the Washington trip was relatively uneventful. But for Xi’s own ambitions, China didn’t need much else. At the White House state dinner Thursday, the Chinese leader emphasized the importance of cooperation, in remarks that framed China’s rise as a boon to America rather than a threat. “The friendship between the two peoples is a worthy cause that holds great promise,” he said. “Let us join hands and move forward side by side.” One key difference between May’s meeting and this one was the chaos surrounding Trump’s decision to bar some reporters from the White House, and the impact that had on images being broadcast – a stark contrast to the choreographed, government-approved coverage on Chinese state media. The rhetoric, however, was by and large the same. Xi likened Trump’s signature slogan, “Make America Great Again,” to his own plan for the “Great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation,” a decades-long strategic vision to transform China into a global powerhouse with world-class military, industrial and technological capabilities. But his remarkable progress in achieving those objectives has prompted US officials to take protectionist measures, including restrictions on Chinese imports, investment and use of US technology. Despite what Beijing sees as an attempt to constrain its advancement, China has maintained record exports, strong AI and robotics development, and a firm grip on goods and materials that the US needs, such as rare earth metals. All that grants Xi far more leverage than he had during his last time in Washington, which means that style over substance may be enough for him – for now. A diplomatic replay Given how US-China clashes have upended global geopolitics and supply chains, a stabilization in their relationship earlier this year was already a win to many observers. But this state visit was largely a muted replay of Trump’s time in Beijing in May, which featured grand symbolic gestures without many concrete actions. Since then Trump has faced increasing political pressure, from the protracted war with Iran and rising inflation, ahead of midterms in November. Major TV news networks did not air the meeting, after Trump barred reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House press pool. While a court later overturned the ban, Trump’s actions raised concerns among US and Chinese officials over how the summit would be perceived, according to CNN reporting. Unlike Trump in Beijing, Xi traveled to Washington without a cabal of business executives. Cui Hongjian, an international relations scholar with Beijing Foreign Studies University, told CNN the lack of corporate representation indicated that the US-China relationship had yet to make any substantial breakthroughs in business or trade. “Right now, both sides are still in a phase where they want to stabilize the political situation a bit more,” Cui said. There were also concerns in Beijing that some of Trump’s team were less positive about US-China relations than the US president, Wu Xinbo, a Chinese Foreign Ministry adviser, told CNN. Xi said Thursday that he hoped the US would welcome Chinese companies and business. In his speech, Trump also detailed a long history of trade and friendship between the US and China. “President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure. We’ve never gotten along better,” he said. But beyond the red-carpet welcome and flowery praise, core contentions remained. Sticking points One of Xi’s main priorities is to chip away at US support for Taiwan, which Beijing considers a part of its territory. Bringing the island democracy under Communist Party control is a key component of Xi’s goal for Chinese rejuvenation. In closed-door discussions, the Chinese leader pressed Trump to “oppose” Taiwan’s independence, according to state news agency Xinhua. The US has long been intentionally ambiguous about its stance on Taiwan’s sovereignty, though it is obligated to sell it weapons for self-defense, under the Taiwan Relations Act. China has previously warned that supporting Taiwan independence could lead to military conflict. The US has not issued a statement on Thursday’s meeting. Xi also called on the US to responsibly manage the development of artificial intelligence with China. The ability of cutting-edge AI models to break out of human control has spurred calls for greater oversight, particularly for the US and China as the world’s leading players. While the leaders of America’s biggest AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, have agreed that the race to develop better models needs to slow down, Trump has claimed that the fears over AI are a “hoax” that benefits China. The rapid advancement of Chinese AI, despite US tech export controls, has caused alarm among US officials, who accused Chinese companies of essentially ripping off US models and raised the possibility of sanctions. China threatened to take countermeasures if the US tries to hinder Chinese AI. But on Thursday, Xi’s message was that the relationship didn’t have to come to that. “We should coexist in peace,” he said.

articles.title: War has returned to Ethiopia’s Tigray — and former enemies are now fighting together. What changed?
articles.summary: Nearly four years ago, a peace deal ended the brutal war in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, one of the deadliest conflicts of the 21st century. Now, the violence has returned — but the battle lines have changed.
articles.body: Nearly four years ago, a peace deal ended the brutal war in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, one of the deadliest conflicts of the 21st century. Now, the violence has returned — but the battle lines have changed. Tigrayan rebels are again fighting the federal government, while forces that were once enemies are now fighting side by side. On Wednesday, Tigrayan forces seized three airports controlled by the federal government, while fighting also broke out in the neighboring regions of Amhara and Afar. The hostilities have shattered the 2022 peace agreement that ended a war estimated to have killed around 600,000 people. Relations between the federal government and Tigray’s leaders had been worsening for months. It’s unclear what led to the recent fighting, with both sides offering conflicting accounts. Tigray’s regional government said federal forces attacked first and that it ordered its forces to respond, calling it a “defensive war.” While Getachew Reda, an adviser to Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said the TPLF had launched an “all-out offensive” against government positions in Afar and Amhara and seized the three airports in Tigray, accusing it of taking “irresponsibility to new heights.” The renewed violence this week follows almost two months of smaller clashes. The nongovernmental organization Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) says fighting between Tigrayan and federal forces began near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan on August 1. The two sides also accused each other of starting those clashes. According to ACLED, federal drone strikes and Tigrayan troop deployments followed, with Tigrayan forces moving tanks and artillery south this month. National carrier Ethiopian Airlines has suspended all flights to Tigray after the airport seizures. How did Ethiopia get here? The TPLF was once Ethiopia’s most powerful political force. It dominated the coalition that governed the country for nearly three decades, despite Tigrayans making up a relatively small share of Ethiopia’s population. That changed after Abiy became prime minister in 2018 following years of anti-government protests. He introduced political reforms and made peace with neighboring Eritrea, which won him the Nobel Peace Prize a year later. But relations with the TPLF deteriorated. Abiy replaced the old ruling coalition with his Prosperity Party in 2019; the TPLF refused to join. After national elections were postponed during the Covid-19 pandemic, Tigray held its own regional vote despite objections from Addis Ababa. In November 2020, Tigrayan forces attacked federal military bases in the region. Abiy sent troops in, and Eritrean forces and fighters from Amhara later fought alongside the federal army. By the time the war ended two years later, millions of people had been displaced and parts of Tigray had been pushed into famine. Both sides faced accusations of serious human rights abuses. Why did the peace deal fail? Hostilities came to an end when the federal government and TPLF signed an African Union-brokered agreement in Pretoria, South Africa, on November 2, 2022. Under the deal, Tigrayan forces were to disarm and federal authority would return to the region. Humanitarian aid and basic services would resume, and an interim administration was later set up to govern Tigray until elections. But major disputes remained, including over territory claimed by both Tigray and Amhara and the return of people displaced by the war. Meanwhile, Eritrea, whose soldiers had fought alongside federal forces, was not party to the agreement. “The agreement didn’t collapse overnight — it was systematically hollowed out over three years,” Surafel Getahun, an Ethiopian geopolitics researcher, told CNN. Getahun said both sides bore responsibility. He accused the federal government of failing to fulfill key parts of the agreement, including returning displaced people, and the TPLF of breaching it by retaking control of the regional administration and rebuilding its military forces. The TPLF was also divided by an internal power struggle, which further weakened the peace process. Rival factions emerged around TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael and Reda, the head of the Tigray interim administration who had been a senior TPLF figure. Reda was later expelled from the party by Gebremichael’s faction, and Abiy appointed a new interim leader in April 2025. A month later, Gebremichael’s faction took back control of Tigray’s government. It restored the regional legislature that existed before the war and installed Gebremichael as regional president. On Sunday, the TPLF joined six other armed groups in a new alliance seeking to remove Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration. The alliance includes former enemies who fought on opposite sides of the last war. TPLF spokesman Michael Asgedom told the Associated Press the groups would cooperate politically and militarily. Asked whether joining the alliance violated the Pretoria agreement, Asgedom said the accord was “no longer valid.” The Amhara Fano National Movement fought alongside the federal government against the TPLF during the last war, then turned against it in 2023. The Oromo Liberation Army, which has long fought Abiy’s government in Oromia, is also a member. Reuters reported Wednesday that Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside the Fano group in Amhara and a local armed group in Afar. But Getahun questioned how long the alliance would hold. The TPLF and Fano remain divided over contested territory, particularly Western Tigray, and its members have different political and military goals. “This is a temporary marriage of convenience against a mutual enemy rather than a lasting political agreement,” he said. Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, told Reuters on Monday that the groups had already been working together with financial backing from Eritrea. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated since their forces fought together in the last war, though the Eritrean government has repeatedly denied supporting Ethiopian armed groups. The African Union (AU) said Wednesday that the airport seizures were inconsistent with the Pretoria deal and urged both parties to de-escalate. It also asked for help from former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who helped mediate the 2022 agreement. Could the war spread further? Tigray has yet to recover from the last war, with communities still rebuilding and many displaced people still unable to return home. Ethiopia is already dealing with armed conflicts in Amhara and Oromia, and ACLED says the federal military was “stretched” before the renewed fighting with the TPLF. But the armed groups in the new alliance vary in their fighting capacity, with several lacking the organization or recruits for wider operations and others largely confined to local areas, according to the conflict monitor. There is also the risk of Eritrea’s military becoming involved. Tensions have grown between the two countries over Ethiopia’s push for access to the Red Sea, including through Eritrea’s port of Assab. The AU urged Ethiopia’s neighbors to avoid actions that could fuel the conflict. The region is already grappling with the war in Sudan and longstanding tensions between Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan over the Nile. Getahun warned that the current fighting could become even more devastating than the previous conflict. “A renewed war would likely end up far bloodier and more widespread than the 2020–2022 fighting,” he said. “Immediate de-escalation and dialogue” are now essential, he added, arguing that negotiations remain “the only viable path forward.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia allies line up support as Houthi attacks mount
articles.summary: France is sending military to protect key Yanbu oil terminal; Pakistan and Turkiye to hold military talks with Riyadh.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s allies are rallying to support the country as the Houthi rebels step up attacks.

France confirmed on Friday that it is sending troops to guard the major oil terminal at Yanbu. Meanwhile, Saudi officials are meeting with peers from Pakistan and Turkiye to discuss options under their mutual defence pact .

French President Emmanuel Macron told broadcasters TF1 and France 2 that Paris is to send “soldiers, radars, and defence systems” to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

“Not to involve ourselves in any conflict, but to protect the site,” he said.

Yanbu hosts major oil storage and refining facilities and is connected by the East-West Pipeline, which can carry up to seven million barrels a day.

The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), have repeatedly fired missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world’s largest energy exporter.

On Thursday, the rebel group said it had struck the facilities of state oil firm Aramco in Yanbu, and a “sensitive target” in Riyadh. Saudi forces said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles. Authorities have not confirmed any damage.

The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye met on Thursday to arrange an “urgent meeting” of their military chiefs of staff under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement , which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all, the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement.

They also condemned Houthi attacks that they claimed targeted Mecca and other civilian sites.

However, doubt persists over what action Turkiye and Pakistan might take under the pact, which is yet to be officially triggered. Both of the Saudi allies are heavily involved as mediators seeking to bring an end to the conflicts across the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia’s grand mufti called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis, according to the Saudi state news agency.

The Iran-aligned Houthis have been battling the Saudi-backed government of Yemen for more than a decade. That conflict has been rekindled amid Israel’s wars against the Iran-aligned Hamas group in Gaza and the Hezbollah group in Lebanon, and the United States war on Iran.

At the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Yemen’s Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al-Alimi-Bawzer warned that the Houthis were using shipping security “as a tool for blackmail”.

“It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” he said.

The US has not renewed military involvement, but Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud said the kingdom was “continuing to work with our partners in the US”.

The Houthi targeting of Yanbu adds to the pressure on Saudi Arabia’s oil exports.

Earlier this month, the Houthis seized the Yemeni port of Mocha and several Red Sea islands, giving them significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, which usually carries about 12 percent of global oil trade.

Strikes have also disrupted the operation of the East-West Pipeline linking Yanbu to export routes. Riyadh had been using it to export crude bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, which is restricted amid the Iran-US war.

However, the Houthis have now forced the Saudis to switch some exports back to Hormuz.

Brent crude rose more than 3 percent on Thursday, briefly topping $108 a barrel, before easing to $105.77 on Friday morning.

June Goh, a senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities in Singapore, said oil would likely stay above $100 a barrel as long as the war on Iran continued.

“With no clear resolution in sight, the gap in oil inventories globally is getting wider,” Goh told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Men charged after UK's second largest ketamine haul found in Upton
articles.summary: Police say the drugs, with an estimated value of £10m, were found in black bin bags.
articles.body:
Three men have been charged after police seized what is believed to be the UK's second-largest haul of ketamine.

West Yorkshire Police said 500kg (1,102lb) of the drug, worth an estimated £10m, was found at a property on Rose Avenue in the the Upton area of Pontefract. The largest find was worth an estimated £17m and was found in Merseyside in 2025.

The force said 20 black bin bags were found during the West Yorkshire operation, led by the Regional Organised Crime Unit.

Curtis Binns, 32, Paul Turner, 40, both from Upton and Christopher Willis, 42, from Wolverhampton, have been charged with drugs offences and are due to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court later.

Police said Binns, 32, of Sunny Avenue, had been charged with possession of a Class B drug with intent to supply and money laundering.

Turner, of Common Lane, had been charged with possession of a Class B drug with intent to supply while Willis had been charged with supplying a Class B drug.

Ketamine is commonly used as a horse tranquiliser.

When abused, the drug can cause serious health problems including permanent bladder damage that can require lifelong treatment.

articles.title: Cut the bull: The real reason beef costs so much — and what Trump is trying to do
articles.summary: Ground beef hit a record $6.92 per pound as the U.S. cattle herd falls to a 75-year low, and Trump signed executive orders targeting beef industry reform.
articles.body: Ground beef just hit a record $6.92 a pound, nearly 60% more than Americans were paying just five years ago. For millions of families, beef isn't a rib eye at a steakhouse; it's the largest source of protein in their diet. It's hamburgers on the grill, taco night, meatloaf, a roast in the crockpot. America didn't forget how to raise cattle. We made it harder to do it, and American families are paying the price for a country that won't let its own ranchers feed it. ‘WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?’: TRUMP'S FOREIGN BEEF PUSH IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN The Trump administration is attempting to bring relief quickly. A temporary order took effect Sept. 1, expanding lower-tariff access for 300,000 metric tons of imported lean beef trimmings, putting more beef in the market while the herd rebuilds. It did not go over well in ranching country. Producers argue that flooding the market with cheaper foreign beef pushes cattle prices down at the very moment American ranchers need stronger prices to justify rebuilding the herd. But the question has never been how much beef we should import. The real question is why it can be cheaper to raise and process beef on the other side of the world, ship it thousands of miles to America and sell it here than to simply produce it at home. Yes, American wages are higher. American beef is also the best in the world, and Americans have shown they'll pay for that. But none of that fully answers the question. Here's what does: foreign beef can cross an ocean and land on a shelf in New York City more easily than a Nebraska rancher's beef can cross the state line into Iowa. A rancher who has his cattle processed under his own state's inspection program, one the USDA has certified as equal to the federal standard, still can't sell that meat one mile over the border. The bureaucracy has built a system where importing is simpler than selling to a neighboring state. And that is only part of the problem. Just look at beef processing. Four companies, two of them Brazilian-owned, control roughly 85% of American beef processing capacity, up from 36% in 1980. This isn't the free market. Crushing regulations, excessive permitting and the capital cost of running a federally compliant plant are so steep that only a handful of operations can absorb them. This is a government-enabled monopoly. A small processor can't open a competing plant, so the giants stay giants, and cattle producers finishing and selling fed cattle across enormous stretches of the country are left with one or two buyers. A producer without competition for offtake doesn't set the price. He takes the only one he's handed. The same scenario shows up again when a rancher tries to tap the free market and sell straight to locals who actually want his beef. A neighbor who wants to buy a quarter of beef directly from the rancher down the road can't just buy it. The animal has to go through an inspected facility, and if the nearest one is hours away and booked out for months, that transaction simply doesn't happen. Ranchers who could be selling directly to consumers at a fair price, cutting out the distant packer entirely, are blocked not by a lack of demand but by a lack of anywhere nearby to legally get the job done. BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS The American cattle herd is at a 75-year low, and U.S. beef production is falling while Brazil has overtaken us as the world's largest beef producer. And ranchers themselves are disappearing. From 2017 to 2022 alone, the number of U.S. farms with beef cows fell by nearly 107,000. American ranchers cannot compete until the barriers putting them at a disadvantage are torn down. That is exactly what President Trump is now trying to do. TRUMP WILL WELCOME FARMERS AND RANCHERS TO WHITE HOUSE DINNER TO CELEBRATE TRADE, TAX WINS On September 4, he signed two executive orders aimed at strengthening American ranching and expanding competition in the beef market. The orders direct federal agencies to reduce regulatory barriers, expand opportunities for state-inspected meat to move across state lines, support smaller and regional processors, modernize inspections and give ranchers more options for processing and selling their own beef. And just last week, USDA took another step, announcing plans to help states start or expand their own meat-inspection programs, opening the door for more local processors to compete and giving ranchers more options for getting their beef to market. These reforms go straight at the problem by creating more processing capacity, giving ranchers more ways to sell and cutting the red tape standing between American beef and American consumers. None of this is unique to beef. Federal timber harvests are down roughly 75% from their 1960-1990 average, even as national forests sit full of standing timber. It now takes seven to 10 years on average to permit a new mine in the United States, compared to two to three years in Canada. We bury American industry under bureaucracy until it's cheaper to buy the finished product from somewhere else. Decades of regulation have put one of America's oldest industries at a systemic disadvantage. Ranchers don't need a handout. articles.title: Pope Leo XIV arrives in France with a message of peace and human dignity
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV began a four-day visit to France, hoping to draw attention to his appeals for peace at a time of war, and reflection on artificial intelligence.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV began a four-day visit to France on Friday, hoping to draw attention to his appeals for peace at a time of war, and for greater reflection as artificial intelligence questions the very essence of what it means to be human. Leo is spending four intense days in Paris, the Catholic shrine at Lourdes and the northeastern city of Metz. Church bells across France tolled when Leo’s charter flight landed at Paris’ Orly airport, and upward of a million people are expected to turn out to see him during his visit. The welcome has underscored the surprising level of interest in Leo’s visit, the first by a pope in 18 years. Leo was greeted by President Emmanuel Macron at the airport and will meet again at the Élysée Palace. During his busiest day of the trip, Leo was to then deliver a speech at UNESCO headquarters, celebrate vespers at the newly reopened Notre-Dame cathedral and then preside over a massive youth vigil at the Paris stadium Friday night. A capstone visit as Macron’s term ends For Macron, who is barred from seeking a third term in May elections, hosting the American pope is something of a capstone, after Pope Francis refused repeatedly to make a proper state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate. “For a president of the republic as Macron, who is at the end of his mandate, it can be important to be aside the pope and to capture a part of his popularity. It’s not new,” said Charles Mercier, director of history and sociology of Catholicism studies at Paris EPHE university. Leo to appeal to loftier questions about life Leo seems keen to emphasize Europe’s Christian roots and try to push the church’s message about the value and dignity of human life in a country where the right to abortion was enshrined in the Constitution in 2024 and where lawmakers recently gave final approval to a bill allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. The French Catholic hierarchy strongly opposed the measures, in keeping with Catholic teaching that human life must be protected and defended from conception until natural death. But the French hierarchy has lost much of its influence amid the secularizing trends at play across Western Europe as well as a credibility crisis stemming from France’s reckoning with its legacy of clergy sexual abuse. France’s distinctive model of secularism, known as laïcité and enshrined in its Constitution, guarantees the freedom to believe or not to believe, as well as the freedom to practice a religion as long as it doesn’t disturb public order. It also requires the state to remain neutral toward all religions. Key rules have been defined by a historic 1905 law, primarily intended to distance the state from the then-powerful influence of the Catholic Church. Leo, whose paternal ancestors were French, isn’t expected to scold the French over the abortion and end-of-life legislation. Rather, he’s expected to summon them to a fundamental, higher-altitude consideration about what it means to be human today, said the Vatican’s editorial director Andrea Tornielli. “The pope is not landing in the City of Light to condemn anyone, nor to barge into the French political debate, which is as polarized as that of every other European country,” Tornielli wrote in Vatican News. “He comes as a shepherd to meet a people, their history, and their culture.” High security reminiscent of Olympics Olympic-level security measures were being put in place, including mounted police, bomb disposal experts, anti-drone measures and counter-terrorism measures, said Paris police prefecture spokesperson Hélène Denéchère. In Paris alone, plans called for 14,000 police officers, gendarmes, and military personnel and 2,500 firefighters on Friday. On Saturday, when Leo celebrates Mass at the central Place de la Concorde, the numbers are only slightly lower. “We are implementing a system similar to what was in place during the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games, which means a protective perimeter around which other security perimeters will be added,” Denéchère said.

articles.title: Why Generation Z is less likely to view China as a threat
articles.summary: Recent research on American attitudes toward China reveal stark generational divides. When asked if China’s growing presence on the world stage is a “critical threat,” 34 percent of Gen Z respondents agreed, compared to 43 percent of Millennials, according to an August survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs. articles.body:
Recent research on American attitudes toward China reveal stark generational divides.

When asked if China’s growing presence on the world stage is a “critical threat,” 34 percent of Gen Z respondents agreed, compared to 43 percent of Millennials, according to an August survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs.

Older generations were much warier, with 56 percent of Gen X and 62 percent of Boomers concerned about Chinese dominance.

Craig Kafura, the director of public opinion and foreign policy at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, suggests that older and younger Americans have simply seen different Chinas.

“For baby boomers, for Gen Xers, these are folks who remember the Cold War. They remember China as this major Communist rival,” Kafura told The Hill.

For Gen Z in particular, Kafura said, “China is a booming economy. Maybe your first introduction to China was the 2008 Olympics in Beijing.”

“That’s a very different mental image of China than somebody who grew up the same time as Mao,” he added.

Americans of all ages, however, are warming up to their rival in the East.

In new data released Wednesday , Pew Research Center asked respondents to rate their feelings on China using a 0 (very cold) to 100 (very warm) scale and found that, on average, Americans give China a 37. In 2021, just after the coronavirus pandemic, that figure was 28.

The survey also found that younger generations hold a more positive opinion of Beijing.

Laura Silver, an associate director at Pew who led the research, provided an explanation for the generational differences similar to Kafura’s.

“Older people knew China as kind of Red China, China under Mao, Tiananmen. Younger people have never had that context,” she told The Hill. Instead, Gen Z knows China as a “superpower that rivals the United States.”

“And I do think that those types of differences in terms of what you knew about China as you were coming of age do play a role and speak to the fact that we’ve seen age differences in our polling for two decades,” she added.

Tuned out: Gen Z values press freedom but steers away from traditional media

Gen Z, notoriously known as passive news consumers, actually values press freedom more than other generations .

In a new Pew Research Center report , 57 percent of adults 18-29 said it is more important for the press to be free to report the news, even if some reporting is inaccurate. In comparison, 43 percent of adults 30-49 and 42 percent of adults 50-plus said the same.

Gen Z was also least likely to say that the government should be able to take down a news story if it poses a risk to national security, contains false information or is critical of the government, at 52 percent, 45 percent and 8 percent, respectively.

Older generations leaned more toward government intervention. Baby boomers, for example, responded with 66 percent, 53 percent and 11 percent, respectively.

“When people are forced to reckon with these circumstances, they tend to defer to the notion that there should be some intervention in place,” Kirsten Eddy, a senior researcher at Pew, told The Hill.

Last week, President Trump revoked White House access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico. He accused the outlets of making “false statements about the war.”

Gen Z actually sees Trump has having a better relationship with the media than older Americans.

Fifteen percent of Gen Z classified the Trump administration’s relationship with U.S. news media as somewhat or very good, compared to 11 percent for Millennials and 10 percent for Gen X. (Baby Boomers were at 9 percent.)

This doesn’t mean that young adults are under generational delusion; it instead showcases the dramatic shift in their news consumption. Gen Z is less likely to seek news out than older generations. Instead, stories pop up via influencers and social media algorithms. They’re also more likely to support advocacy journalism and journalists who also share opinions, per Eddy.

According to a Navigator study , 52 percent of Gen Z passively seeks out news, compared to 43 percent of Millennials, 40 percent of Gen X and 31 percent of Boomers. This generational shift is a trend, Tina Tang, director of polling and analytics at Navigator, told The Hill.

Researchers also conducted qual boards — a private online forum — and engaged passive news consumers on their media diets. Participants listed an array of online outlets and creators that kept them informed.

“For a lot of these passive news consumers, they engage in a different way. Just because they’re passive, especially for Gen Z, it doesn’t mean they don’t care about politics,” Tang said. “They’re siloed, but not as siloed as we think.”

Gen Z job trends: Nearly 3 in 4 Gen Z healthcare workers are looking for an escape from their current role

Gen Zers are no stranger to “job hopping.”

Young adults’ average tenure at a job within the first five years of their career is only 1.1 years, according to a 2025 report from Randstand .

But one industry is particularly affected: healthcare.

A September 2026 study from The Harris Poll showed that 70 percent of Gen Z healthcare workers are actively searching for their next job within the industry.

This comes as the Health Resources and Services Administration projects the U.S. will face a shortage of 500,000 healthcare workers by 2038.

Adele Webb, a nurse for over 42 years and healthcare workforce advisor at Workforce Edge, which co-commissioned the poll, sees the trend unfold in front of her.

Only 26 percent of Gen Z healthcare workers trust their employer for long-term growth, a 54-point gap between what employers want and what they believe they will actually get.

“The survey shows that trust is low, and I think part of it is that employers don’t understand what it is the employees want, or they can’t figure out a way to provide it,” Webb told The Hill.

Employers are also recognizing the trust gap. Almost half (47 percent) believe a lack of advancement opportunities, career development or education are the main reasons employees leave.

“The trust gap is really concerning because I think it’s one of the things that causes people to burnout or move on,” she added.

Artificial intelligence is also creeping into the industry, with healthcare workers exercising their AI use with caution. Forty-eight percent feel comfortable using AI, and another 39 percent said the technology doesn’t have any impact on their work.

Webb said that respondents said they did not see AI as a threat to their job, but something that could bolster their position. While other fields differ, nurses are more hands-on. “You’re not gonna get that through artificial intelligence,” Webb said.

Webb believes it’s up to Gen Z to ask questions about how they will help advance their career.

“They need to advocate for themselves,” Webb said.

The Harris Poll surveyed 1,514 healthcare employees and 304 healthcare employers between June 12 to July 1, 2026. The margin of error was 3.4 percentage points for employees and 6.7 percent for employers.

articles.title: Scottish emergency heating oil fund extended into winter
articles.summary: The scheme was initially available in Scotland for six months from 1 April.
articles.body:
A fund set up to help lower income households that rely on heating oil and LPG to warm their homes has been extended into winter.

The Scottish Emergency Heating Oil Scheme was introduced for an initial six months on 1 April after conflict in the Middle East drove up prices.

About 142,000 Scottish households use heating oil and average costs soared to 153.74 pence per litre in March and, after dropping over the summer, prices have risen to almost 121 pence per litre . About 27,000 households use LPG.

The Scottish government said there had been more than 6,700 payments from the scheme so far.

Energy Minister Stephen Gethins said the fund would help those in greatest need.

He said: "While prices have fallen since the peak in March, ongoing international uncertainty means further increases cannot be ruled out this winter.

"That is why we are extending the scheme so eligible households can still apply for support if prices remain high over the colder months to come."

Households that use heating oil or LPG have also been encouraged to contact Home Energy Scotland for free and impartial advice on reducing costs.

Head of programme delivery Beth Mukushi said: "As the Scottish government-funded energy advice service, we speak to people in rural homes every day who are looking to make their homes warmer and more energy efficient.

"They may be in off-gas areas, worried about rising energy costs or are in an older property and don't know where to start. That can sometimes feel overwhelming; but we can help."

There is no fixed date for how long the extension to the fund will last and it will be kept under review.

Scottish government figures published last year found that a third of households in the Highlands were living in fuel poverty. In the Western Isles the figure was 40%.

Trump sets out to dazzle Xi despite past criticisms of China President Donald Trump has accused China of hacking America’s elections and plundering its wealth, yet he has showered the visiting Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, with tributes and affection during their summit this week at the White House. In fact, Trump has rolled out the red carpet not once but twice for Xi. And yesterday evening, Trump feted Xi at a state dinner and gave his guest a statue of a bald eagle as a gift. The two presidents were set to discuss trade, the Iran war and AI, among other issues, though foreign policy experts expect no substantive breakthroughs. Those trying to view the summit live may have faced difficulties after Trump imposed a media ban last week on three outlets, prompting other to suspend “pool” coverage of the president’s public events. Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back at the White House yesterday, but pool coverage hadn’t resumed by the afternoon. All the pomp and ceremony may seem confusing considering Trump’s past critiques. He has accused China of meddling in the 2020 election. He has spoken out against communism — but welcomed the leader of the world’s largest communist country. And China may have provided Iran with missiles and technology in the ongoing war. But Trump, who has long believed that personal relationships are key to managing political tensions, has set out to charm the Chinese leader. Read the full story here. The party’s lead, which stands at 52% to 43%, is part of a steady deterioration of the political environment for the GOP, as independent voters have gradually begun to prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress and have soured on Donald Trump. The president’s approval rating has slid to 39% in the NBC News polling average, with 59% disapproving of his job performance so far. At least six babies in the state have been born infected with the virus, with two so sick they had to be admitted into intensive care. The lack of experience treating the disease is “because up until a couple of months ago, it didn’t occur,” an infectious disease expert explained. At least 800 people across most of the state have been infected with measles so far this year. Congenital measles was uncommon before the measles vaccine was introduced in the early 1960s because, at the time, most women had been infected as children. articles.title: West Northants aims to 'safeguard nature' for future generations
articles.summary: Local Nature Recovery Strategy is approved for one of England's "most nature-depleted areas".
articles.body:
More tree planting, wetland restoration and drainage work could take place in parts of Northamptonshire to "safeguard nature for generations to come".

West Northamptonshire Council has approved its first Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) which was required by the Environment Act 2021 and is the responsibility of all authorities.

It said the area was one of England's "most nature-depleted areas" and its wildlife sites "are often small, in poor condition, and isolated from one another".

Working with a range of partners the council hopes to improve landscapes that are "under unprecedented pressure" with some species in decline.

A spokesperson for the council said: "A healthy natural environment is essential for tackling climate change and wider environmental challenges.

"The diversity of habitats and species provide essentials such as clean and plentiful water, food, clean air, productive soil, flood protection, shading and cooling, as well as benefits like space for recreation, exercise and wellbeing."

Nigel Stansfield, Reform UK's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "Our aim is to safeguard nature for generations to come, and create cleaner, greener spaces that meet the needs of local communities and offer them an opportunity to connect with nature."

He said it was vital to have a workable strategy that sets out "how we intend to safeguard nature for generations to come."

Stansfield added he hoped the strategy would get organisations, landowners and local people to take action "to ensure our natural environment becomes more robust and resilient to provide the benefits we often take for granted".

articles.title: Zelensky says Trump has made ‘final decision’ to allow Kyiv to make Patriot missiles
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday that US President Donald Trump will allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot missiles, a key demand as Kyiv tries to fend off relentless Russian aerial attacks.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday that US President Donald Trump will allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot missiles, a key demand as Kyiv tries to fend off relentless Russian aerial attacks. “There are concrete agreements in place,” Zelensky told reporters. “During our last meeting, President Trump emphasized that, yes, I have made the final decision: Ukraine will receive a license to manufacture Patriot missiles.” The two met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week, where Zelensky called his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” saying the more freedom he has to act, “the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.” The question of whether Trump would fulfil his promise to allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptors – a top-tier track-and-destroy defense system Ukrainians hope will cut through Russia’s relentless ballistic missiles strikes – has loomed over Ukraine for months. Trump suggested Ukraine would gain the right to make Patriots on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Turkey back in July, but weeks later he cooled on the offer. CNN has approached the White House for comment. Zelensky also said Washington had proposed organizing three-way talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US. “Regarding the trilateral meeting, the US side proposed organizing it,” Zelensky said, adding that no date had yet been set, and the US had suggested the United Arab Emirates as the location. “We will brief the European side and discuss these details with them, the Americans will talk to the Russians, and in ten days’ time we will return with a particular perspective and a result,” Zelensky said. So far, Russia has made no commitment to trilateral talks, saying only they could happen “soon.” Russia has been hammering Ukraine, and Kyiv in particular, with near constant aerial attacks for around a month. On Friday five civilians including a teenager were killed and at least 27 more injured in a series of daytime drone strikes on Kyiv, according to the capital’s mayor.

articles.title: Xi wrapping up DC visit with trip to see Constitution, Bill of Rights
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping will close out his first state visit to the U.S. in over a decade on Friday with a tour of the National Archives alongside President Trump. The building houses important documents in American history, including the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights. The archives also has an…
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping will close out his first state visit to the U.S. in over a decade on Friday with a tour of the National Archives alongside President Trump.

The building houses important documents in American history, including the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.

The archives also has an exhibit to mark the nation’s 250th anniversary, called “The American Story,” which features nine galleries that spotlight different eras of the country’s history. It includes state gifts from foreign leaders to past U.S. presidents, George Washington’s annotated copy of the draft Constitution and declassified records from the Cuban Missile Crisis.

The Chinese leader will visit the vault of records after beginning his day at the White House for tea with his wife, Peng Liyuan, as well as Trump and first lady Melania Trump.

On Thursday evening, Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner with technology leaders and gave him a tour of the new additions around the executive grounds, including a granite Marine One landing pad and his ballroom construction project.

The two heads of state also held a private meeting in the Oval Office on Thursday, in which they discussed the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to an official Chinese government readout from the meeting. The White House has not provided its own details.

China has repeatedly pressed the U.S. to halt a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan , which Xi’s government considers a Chinese territory. Trump delayed this transaction after his bilateral summit with the leader in May, describing the arms sale as a “very good negotiating chip” with Beijing.

Trump and Xi were also expected to discuss concerns over the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence , as Democratic lawmakers urge the president to place guardrails on the rapidly developing technology and cut off supplies to China.

“Very productive meeting with President Xi for both the U.S.A. and China. Tremendous things will be happening,” the president wrote Friday on Truth Social.

“Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE,” the president, who has dismissed concerns around the risks of growing AI, continued. “That would be “SUPER!” Everyone last night agreed, also.”

articles.title: India’s ‘cockroach’ movement demands election chief’s resignation
articles.summary: Youth group threatens return to mass protests, sets deadline for Gyanesh Kumar to quit over reports of meddling.
articles.body:
India’s ‘cockroach’ party youth movement has threatened to launch nationwide protests unless the country’s chief election officer does not resign by Saturday.

Founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) , Abhijeet Dipke, announced on Friday that protests would begin in Mumbai on October 2 – if Gyanesh Kumar does not step down.

The CJP, a satirical outfit born on Instagram in May after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young Indians to “cockroaches” and “parasites”, has shaken the staunchly conservative government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

On Thursday, the group demanded that Kumar quit within 48 hours, following a newspaper report linking him to altered voter lists. Opposition parties say the lists have been manipulated to benefit Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

“If Gyanesh Kumar does not resign by tomorrow, CJP will begin its nationwide protest from Mumbai on 2 October, and take it to cities across India,” Dipke posted on X.

“This Gandhi Jayanti let’s pledge to save democracy,” he added, referring to the October 2 holiday marking independence leader Mahatma Gandhi’s birthday.

On Wednesday, the Indian Express newspaper reported that two election commissioners had raised questions or voiced concern with Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, mostly over the process of updating voter lists that began last year.

The main opposition Congress party announced protest marches on state election offices across India on Friday, demanding Kumar’s arrest, his removal and an independent review of decisions and voter-list changes made under him.

Opposition parties have long accused the commission of deleting the names of millions of voters without warning and adding new voters without verification to favour the BJP.

The Election Commission of India said that “differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution” and that all its actions were lawful.

The BJP has defended the commission, accusing the opposition of a smear campaign because it keeps losing elections.

“Neither the Election Commission of India nor any constitutional body in India is under dictatorial rule,” BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra said on Wednesday.

CJP-led protests in July forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister over exam-paper leaks, one of the prime minister’s biggest political setbacks since coming to power in 2014.

articles.title: China’s Uyghur crackdown has not ended — it has gone underground
articles.summary: It has become more diffuse, more legally disguised and harder for the world to see.
articles.body:
On Aug. 3, Kaisar Abduqeyum Hoja, a Uyghur translator, died suddenly in his home in Urumqi. His sister, Gulchehra Hoja, a journalist with Radio Free Asia living in the U.S., did not learn of his death until a week later — and then only through intermediaries.

In an age of instant global communication, that week of silence offers a window into how China’s repression of Uyghurs has evolved.

I first met Hoja in 2018, when I was working for Amnesty International in Hong Kong. More than 20 members of her family had been detained, including her elderly parents and her brother Kaisar. Amnesty International launched urgent actions and media campaigns to try to save her family.

At the time, the world was beginning to understand the enormous scale of China’s campaign in the Uyghur region. Beijing had constructed hundreds of so-called vocational and education training centers, which it claimed were designed to combat terrorism. In reality, these re-education camps became part of one of the largest campaigns of mass detention and social engineering of the 21st century.

The camps eventually became the defining image of the crackdown. Under immense international scrutiny, Beijing largely closed the camps in 2019-2020, although many people in the camps were simply sent to prisons .

As attention from the camp system has faded, a dangerous illusion has set in that the repression itself has ended. It has not. The system has evolved.

Hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs who were not sent to the camps were instead imprisoned. The precise number remains unknowable because Beijing does not publish figures, but Chinese authorities reported that more than 540,000 people have been prosecuted in the region since 2017. A comprehensive database documenting individual cases found that roughly 37 percent received sentences of 10 years or more — meaning that enormous numbers remain behind bars.

A United Nations body has offered a glimpse into what happens behind this supposedly legal process. In nine opinions concerning 21 Uyghur individuals since 2016, it found no evidence that they had access to legal counsel.

A similar lawfare strategy is evident in the Uyghur region’s forced labor system. Uyghurs have been transferred in large numbers from their hometowns to factories and farms where they are heavily surveilled. These transfers affect industries ranging from cotton and textiles to automobiles, solar panels and critical minerals.

The United States responded in 2021 with the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act , which created a rebuttable presumption that goods tied to the region were produced with forced labor unless companies could prove otherwise. But Beijing has raided auditing firms investigating forced labor allegations.

Most recently, the Chinese government issued orders that restrict information gathering in its supply chains. It sanctioned six U.S. organizations involved in supply-chain risk assessment after Washington added Chinese entities to its forced labor enforcement list.

Beijing has also used the insidious tool of isolation.

The Uyghur region has become one of the world’s most sophisticated surveillance environments. Families separated across borders therefore cannot communicate normally. As research from the Uyghur Human Rights Project has shown , Uyghur “families are prevented from normal communications both directly, through intimidation and monitored calls, and indirectly, through fear of reprisals for attempting to maintain contact.”

Even family visits can become instruments of control. The Uyghur Transitional Justice Database found that returning overseas Uyghurs were interrogated by police before being allowed to visit their relatives and were incentivized to provide information on ideologically “misaligned” Uyghurs abroad. Similarly, Human Rights Watch recently found that overseas Uyghurs were compelled by Chinese agents to gather information about Uyghur language schools in the diaspora.

In effect, China is turning family ties into leverage.

The dismantling of the camps therefore does not mean the end of repression. It has become more diffuse, more legally disguised and harder for the world to see. The Chinese government wants to convince the world that speaking up against repression is useless. It is not. Hoja learned years later that the 2018 urgent action campaign helped ensure that her family received extra milk and eggs while in the camps.

Actions taken now can have similarly profound ripple effects.

But facing an authoritarian superpower, Uyghurs can’t achieve justice alone. Uyghur friends repeatedly emphasize commonsense points of action for the international community. Those are vigorously tackling transnational repression, demanding the release of unjustly imprisoned Uyghurs, such as entrepreneur Ekpar Asat and retired physician Gulshan Abbas , ensuring American allies enact forced labor import bans based on the U.S. model and holding the Chinese government accountable for its crimes against humanity.

None of this is easy. But silence will ensure that repression wins out.

William Nee is the senior program manager for East Asia at the National Endowment for Democracy.
